headline: Niantic boats grinding fluke at 40 feet — Black Point sea bass steady, stripers gone nocturnal
subhead: The eastern Sound is running a few degrees cooler than the rest of the water and it's holding the bite together while everyone else deals with dead-warm surface temps.
body_markdown:
Ran into one of the mates off the Waterford fleet at the bait shop Thursday morning loading up on squid and spearing, and he told me straight up: "We're not setting the world , but we're not getting skunked either." That's about the most honest summary of this week you're gonna get, and it tracks with everything I'm seeing and hearing up and down this stretch.

The drift boats out of Niantic have settled into a groove on fluke in about 38 to 42 feet off the bay mouth and out toward Twotree Island Channel. It's not a bang-bang bite — more like work for your fish, mixed shorts with enough keepers in the 19 to 22 inch range to make the trip worth it. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4 to 1-ounce bucktails are still the go-to, tipped with a strip of squid for scent, dragged slow on the tail end of the drift where the current's easing off. Guys who are marking bait on the sounder and slowing the drift down with a sea anchor are doing noticeably better than the ones bombing through the same water at full drift speed. Fluke this time of year get lazy in the heat — you gotta bring the bait to them, not make them chase.

Black sea bass have been the most dependable thing going. Black Point and the rock piles off Hole-in-the-Wall are stacked with them, and they're mixing right into the fluke drifts as a bonus that's honestly outproducing the target species some days. Double-hook bottom rigs with Asian squid strips or clam, dropped right on the reef edges on the last two hours of the incoming, that's the play. Fish are running a good average size too — plenty of 14 to 16 inchers, some pushing 17. Porgies are thick in Niantic Bay proper, especially around the mooring fields and out toward McCook Point, and if you've got kids or you just want a bucket of dinner fish, sandworms or clam on a high-low rig in 15 to 20 feet will keep the rod bouncing all afternoon.

Now here's the thing that's shaping everything right now — the thermal gradient across the Sound. Kings Point is reading close to 71 degrees, New London's sitting around 69.4. That two-degree difference doesn't sound like much, but it matters. The western and central Sound is running warm enough that stripers out there have gone almost entirely nocturnal, pushed deep and feeding mostly after dark. Out here, we're cooler, and that's kept a little more daytime activity going, though it's far from the wide-open bite you'd want. I'm still telling guys the best striper play right now is first light and last light, working eels or fresh bunker chunks on the drop-offs around Black Point and the deeper cuts in Twotree Channel. Daytime, if you want a shot, go deep — 25 to 35 feet, slow-trolled bunker spoons or umbrella rigs, right on the current seams. It's a grind, not a guarantee, but the fish are there if you put the time in on the right stage of tide.

Bluefish have been the one bright spot that doesn't require finesse. Schools have been running through Hole-in-the-Wall and pushing up into the mouth of the Niantic River chasing bunker, and when they show up top it's an easy game — diamond jigs, or if you want the fun version, poppers and Kastmasters worked fast across the surface. Sizes have been solid, a lot of 3 to 5 pounders with some bigger choppers mixed in, which lines up with what's been happening for the fleets to our west — there's a fresh wave of blues pushing down the coast and this stretch of the Sound is getting its share.

Tide-wise, we're building toward the new moon, and that's worth paying attention to over the next week or two. Stronger current means better current edges, better bait concentration, and it's exactly the kind of setup that can trigger the first false albacore push into this end of the Sound. I flagged this a couple weeks back — said this zone was worth watching given how close we sit to the Race and the Fishers Island corridor — and while nobody's connected on an albie here yet, the ingredients are lining up. Squid are building around the Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound side, current's about to get stronger with the building tides, and that's the recipe that usually brings the first fall speedster sightings into Fishers Island Sound and eventually our way. I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet, but if you're out there anyway working blues or bass, keep a rod rigged with a small metal or an epoxy jig, just in case something silver and fast rips through the bait.

Look-ahead for the week: I'd stick with the fluke/sea bass combo drifts on the calmer tide stages, work stripers on the edges at dawn and dusk rather than midday, and keep an eye on Hole-in-the-Wall for bluefish blitzes when the bunker pods show. If the wind stays out of the south and the water holds steady, this pattern should carry through the coming week pretty much as-is. A cold front or a stretch of northerly wind could stir the deeper bass out of their nighttime funk and back into a more normal daytime pattern — that's the wildcard I'd watch for.
